title: Third-party standing and its relationship to associations
shortTitle: Third-party standing and its relationship to associations
summary: A claimant asserting another person’s rights ordinarily needs its own injury, an obstacle to the right-holder’s own suit, and an appropriate representative relationship.
notes:
The casebook identifies three considerations for third-party rights claims: injury to the plaintiff from denial of the other person’s rights, an obstacle to that person’s independent assertion, and an appropriate representative relationship. It contrasts physicians permitted to challenge Medicaid exclusions affecting patients in Singleton with a pediatrician denied standing as doctor, parent, and defender of the unborn in Diamond. The brief descriptions establish the comparison but do not reproduce each complete opinion.

Associational standing supplies a more developed route for organized groups representing members, with the Hunt requirements explained in Brock. The doctrines overlap in representational concerns but have distinct formulations. The question also appears in Newport News, where an administrator sought to litigate a claimant’s benefits determination, and in the dissent to Biden v. Nebraska, where Missouri sued despite MOHELA’s absence. Identifying whose injury and whose legal right are at issue is the necessary starting point.
